# Field guide to the river walk

This guide follows the river path from the old mill to the estuary, about eleven kilometres on level ground. It describes what you will pass, where to stop, and what to look for in each season. Distances are measured from the mill gate, and the numbered posts along the path match the sections below.

## The mill gate

The walk starts at the gate of the old flour mill, which ground grain for the valley from the early eighteenth century until a fire closed it in 1931. The wheel pit is still visible behind the railings, and in wet weather the overflow channel runs fast enough to hear from the car park. A map board by the gate shows the whole route and the four places where buses stop near the path.

From the gate, the path drops down a short ramp to the water and turns left under the road bridge. The bridge arches are low, so taller walkers should mind their heads, and after heavy rain the towpath under the first arch can be muddy for a week or more.

## Post 1: the weir

Half a kilometre downstream, the weir holds back the mill pond. Herons stand on the sloping face in the early morning, waiting for fish carried over the lip, and in autumn salmon can sometimes be seen trying the fish pass on the far bank. The bench at the top of the steps faces the weir and is the best place to watch them.

The weir was rebuilt in stone in 1820 after the timber one before it washed away. A plaque on the parapet records the flood level of that winter, well above head height, which gives some idea of how much water the valley can carry.

## Post 2: the water meadows

Below the weir the valley opens out into water meadows, flooded on purpose each winter for three centuries to bring an early crop of grass. The channels and sluices that controlled the water still cross the fields, and the path follows a raised bank between them. In May the meadows are full of buttercups and the low ditches are loud with frogs.

Please keep dogs on a lead through the meadows from March to July, when ground-nesting birds are raising their young. Lapwings and skylarks both breed here, and a single disturbance can make a parent leave the nest for long enough that the eggs go cold.

## Post 3: the ferry steps

At three kilometres a flight of worn steps leads down to the water where a rowing ferry crossed until 1954. The ferryman's cottage on the far bank is now a private house, but the bell he answered still hangs on its post at the top of the steps. Ringing it is discouraged, as the present owners have heard it often enough.

The river here is deep and slow, and it is one of the few places along the walk where kingfishers can be seen reliably. Look for a flash of blue low over the water, usually heading downstream, and listen for the short high whistle they give in flight.

## Post 4: the railway viaduct

The viaduct carries the main line across the valley on twenty-one brick arches. It was finished in 1847 and took four years and more than eleven million bricks, most of them made from clay dug from the pits that are now the fishing lakes to the east. Trains still cross it every few minutes, and the sound of them carries a long way down the valley.

Under the seventh arch from the north there is a small display about the navvies who built it, with a list of the men known to have died during the work. The display was put together by the local history society from parish records and newspaper reports of the time.

## Post 5: the fishing lakes

The old clay pits filled with water when the brickworks closed, and they are now managed as fishing lakes and a nature reserve. A hide on the largest lake is open to everyone from dawn to dusk, and a board inside lists the birds seen that week. Winter is the best season, when ducks and geese arrive from further north.

Anglers need a permit from the lodge by the car park, and fishing is allowed only from the marked swims. The lakes are deep close to the banks, so children should be watched carefully, and swimming is not allowed at any time of year.

## Post 6: the lock

At six kilometres the path reaches the only lock on this stretch, built when the lower river was made navigable for barges carrying coal up from the coast. The lock keeper's house beside it serves teas at weekends from Easter to October, and the garden tables look straight down the lock to the river below.

The gates are worked by hand, and on summer weekends it is common to see a narrowboat passing through. Crews are usually happy to explain what they are doing, and visitors are welcome to help push the balance beams if they are asked.

## Post 7: the reed beds

Beyond the lock the river widens into reed beds that stretch nearly to the estuary. A boardwalk carries the path across the wettest part, and from it you can hear reed warblers in summer and see marsh harriers hunting low over the reeds in almost every month of the year.

The reeds were once cut every winter for thatching, and a few local thatchers still take a harvest from the eastern beds. Cutting in rotation keeps the beds healthy, because old reed left standing for many years slowly turns the wetland into scrub and then into wet woodland.

## Post 8: the sea wall

The last two kilometres follow the sea wall, an earth bank built to keep the tide off the grazing marshes behind it. From the top you can see across the mudflats to the estuary mouth and, on a clear day, the lighthouse on the far headland. The wind here is stronger than anywhere else on the walk, so bring a layer even in summer.

At low tide the mudflats are covered with feeding wading birds, and at high tide they gather on the shingle spit at the end of the wall to wait for the water to fall. Please keep well back from the roosting flocks, because every time they are put up they use energy they need for the winter.

## The estuary

The walk ends at the harbour, where the river meets the sea between two stone piers. Buses back to the mill leave from the stop outside the harbour office every half hour until early evening, and the timetable is posted inside the office window. The fish market on the quay is open in the mornings except on Sundays.

If you have time, the small museum in the old customs house tells the story of the port, from the coal barges that came down the river to the fishing fleet that worked out of the harbour until the 1970s. Entry is free, and the volunteers who run it are glad of questions.

## Seasons on the path

Each season changes the walk. In spring the meadows flower and the birds are nesting, so the path is best walked quietly and with dogs on leads. Summer brings the longest days and the busiest weekends, with boats at the lock and families at the lakes. Autumn is the time for salmon at the weir and fungi in the woods below the viaduct.

Winter is the quietest season and, for many regular walkers, the best. The flooded meadows reflect the sky, the lakes fill with ducks and geese, and the estuary is crowded with waders. Days are short, so start early, and check the tide table before setting out along the sea wall.

## Looking after the path

The path is maintained by volunteers from the river trust, who clear fallen trees, repair the boardwalk and empty the litter bins. If you see a problem, the number to call is on every map board. Donations to the trust pay for materials and for the small team of rangers who coordinate the volunteers through the year.

Above all, please take your litter home, close the gates behind you, and leave the plants and animals as you found them. The river walk has been enjoyed by people from the valley for generations, and with a little care it will stay that way for those who come after us.
